sources.quote: who are of a type/specialty that is legally eligible to order and refer Part B (clinical laboratory and imaging), DME and HHA claims, in the Medicare program and who have current enrollment records in Medicare
sources.searcher_note: The file's own documentation: it should list only clinicians with current Medicare enrollment, updated twice a week; also says deceased clinicians are excluded. States the rule the lead tests; does not report any gap.

sources.quote: This only applies to items in capped rental category, all other items will be denied after the deactivation date and a new ordering physician would be required for all other items.
sources.searcher_note: Contractor claim-edit rule: capped rental items keep paying up to 13 months after the ordering physician's PECOS deactivation; everything else denied. A designed grace window relevant to the lead's caveat. Names PECOS edits, not the O&R file.

sources.quote: Additionally, provider data were inconsistent between NPPES and PECOS for 97 percent of records.
sources.searcher_note: Pattern: NPPES (where NPIs are deactivated) and PECOS (which feeds the ordering list) disagree for nearly all records. Not about the O&R file or DME flag specifically.

sources.outlet: Office of Sen. Susan Collins (Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations release)
sources.quote: The Subcommittee’s investigation found that Medicare paid as much as $92 million over the past seven years for durable medical equipment such as wheelchairs, prosthetics, hospital beds, and other home medical equipment purportedly prescribed by physicians.
sources.searcher_note: Pattern: DME (incl. wheelchairs) paid on orders under dead doctors' IDs, 2000-2007. Predates the ordering/referring edits and the O&R file.

sources.outlet: CHAP (Community Health Accreditation Partner), The Compliance Monitor
sources.quote: The paper outlines strategic actions to address these vulnerabilities, including strengthening enrollment safeguards, leveraging modern data analytics to catch fake physician orders, and expanding protections for enrollee identification numbers.
sources.searcher_note: Post-cutoff pattern coverage: summarizes an OIG white paper on DME fraud via enrolled suppliers, physician orders and beneficiary IDs. Does not mention deactivated clinicians or the ordering list.

notes: No source found reports that the O&R file keeps recently deactivated clinicians eligible to order DME, or the 1,036 of 1,247 / 83% vs 2 of 1,040 / 0.2% contrast, or the power-wheelchair flag rate. The file's own methodology says it lists only current enrollees. The Noridian page documents a designed 13-month post-deactivation window for capped rentals only, relevant to the lead's 'grace window vs hole' caveat. Other material is pattern only (deceased-doctor DME orders 2008; NPPES/PECOS mismatch 2013; OIG DME-fraud white paper 2026). A search snippet quoted 42 CFR 424.540 as barring ordering while deactivated, but eCFR redirected to a block page and the Cornell copy did not show that sentence; not recorded. OIG A-02-20-01027 (Part C/D payments to deactivated providers) opened; off-measure, not recorded.
